# **Frontier Research in Agentic Computer-Aided Design: Multi-Agent Workflows, Physics-Aware Verification, and Programmatic DSLs**

Computer-Aided Design (CAD) is undergoing a major paradigm shift, evolving from a manual, expertise-intensive engineering workflow into an autonomous computational discipline1. Historically, automated design methodologies relied either on rigid parametric scripts bound by predefined rule sets or on generative deep learning models—such as 3D diffusion networks and neural implicit representations—that synthesize unconstrained meshes or point clouds2. Although deep learning models produce visually plausible 3D shapes, mesh-based outputs lack the underlying construction history, parametric editability, and boundary representation (B-Rep) topological precision required for industrial manufacturing1.  
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as autonomous agents has established a new frontier in programmatic CAD generation1. By driving execution environments such as CadQuery, OpenCASCADE, and FreeCAD, agentic architectures bridge the gap between high-level natural language specifications and low-level geometric kernels1. However, early single-pass code generation by monolithic LLMs suffered from frequent API misuse, dimensional hallucinations, invalid topological operations, and non-watertight geometry1.  
To overcome these failure modes, contemporary research has converged on four foundational pillars:

* Role-specialized multi-agent architectures featuring closed-loop execution and visual verification1.  
* Stateful execution harnesses leveraging protocol standards like the Model Context Protocol (MCP)7.  
* Physics-in-the-loop simulation loops using Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and Technology CAD (TCAD) engines6.  
* Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) designed to decouple high-level topological intent from deterministic geometric solving10.

## **Role-Specialized Multi-Agent Frameworks and Closed-Loop Refinement Protocols**

The limitations of monolithic, single-pass text-to-CAD models have driven the adoption of role-specialized multi-agent pipelines1. By decomposing complex design tasks into dedicated sub-tasks—such as prompt parsing, code generation, sandboxed execution, geometric validation, and iterative refinement—agentic frameworks reduce syntactic and spatial failure rates1.  
A representative architecture in multi-agent programmatic design is CADSmith, which decomposes the text-to-CAD pipeline into five autonomous agents operating across two nested correction loops1. Rather than relying on end-to-end model fine-tuning, CADSmith employs Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over API documentation and error-pattern knowledge bases, enabling the system to adapt as underlying CAD libraries evolve1.  
The framework distributes responsibilities across five specialized agent roles1:

* The Planner Agent converts raw natural language prompts into a structured JSON design plan, extracting sub-component hierarchies, target bounding box dimensions (![][image1] in millimeters), and explicit geometric constraints1.  
* The Coder Agent synthesizes executable CadQuery Python code based on the structured plan, retrieving API syntax and usage examples from a dedicated documentation knowledge base1.  
* The Executor Agent runs generated scripts within a sandboxed, isolated Python subprocess1. Upon successful compilation, it exports B-Rep models into STEP and STL formats while extracting exact kernel-level measurements directly from OpenCASCADE1.  
* The Validator Agent operates as a VLM-as-a-Judge, utilizing an advanced vision model (such as Claude Opus) to prevent self-confirmation bias from the generator model1. It cross-references four inputs: the original prompt, the generated code, OpenCASCADE kernel metrics, and rendered images1.  
* The Refiner Agent formulates targeted parameter and topological fixes when validation fails, consuming execution tracebacks or kernel mismatch reports1.

System reliability is governed by two hierarchical feedback loops1. The Inner Execution Correction Loop activates when the Executor captures Python syntax errors or CadQuery API tracebacks1. An Error Refiner agent queries a specialized error database containing classified failure modes—such as fillet radius violations, unclosed wires, arc construction errors, and invalid selectors—to correct the script within a maximum of three retries1.  
The Outer Geometric Refinement Loop triggers when code executes cleanly but yields incorrect geometry1. Operating up to five iterations, the Refiner receives structured numerical feedback from OpenCASCADE kernel metrics—including volume, bounding box dimensions, center of mass, face/edge/vertex counts, and solid validity—alongside three VTK-rendered images (isometric view, high-angle rear view, and front profile view)1. Hard kernel checks override visual checks: if OpenCASCADE reports a non-watertight or invalid solid, the iteration is automatically failed1. At iteration three and beyond, explicit escalation guidance prompts the Refiner to modify the overarching construction strategy rather than fine-tuning micro-parameters1.

| Metric | Single-Pass Zero-Shot Baseline | CADSmith (Full Multi-Agent Pipeline) | Performance Delta / Significance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Code Execution Success Rate** | 95.0% | **100.0%** | Complete elimination of runtime API crashes via inner loop1 |
| **Median Volumetric IoU** | 0.8085 | **0.9629** | \+19.1% improvement in spatial volumetric accuracy1 |
| **Median Mesh F1 Score (![][image2])** | 0.9707 | **0.9846** | Enhanced dimensional precision across tight manufacturing tolerances1 |
| **Mean Chamfer Distance (![][image3])** | 28.37 ![][image4] | **0.74 ![][image4]** | 97.4% reduction in overall geometric spatial deviation1 |
| **First-Iteration Convergence** | N/A | **88.0%** | 88/100 benchmark tasks pass validation on iteration zero1 |

## **Stateful Environments and Protocol-Driven Interactive CAD Editing**

Beyond single-part synthesis, contemporary research emphasizes interactive editing of persistent CAD models7. Modern industrial design relies on iterative modifications based on multimodal user requests7. Conventional conversational LLM architectures struggle with state tracking over long editing sessions, often regenerating entire programs and introducing unintended side effects into non-targeted features7.  
Frameworks such as AgenticCADedit resolve state degradation by placing the LLM inside a stateful execution environment governed by the Model Context Protocol (MCP)7. Operating as an MCP server subprocess, the harness maintains a single persistent Python namespace7. It imports CadQuery once and retains variable references across multi-turn interactions, allowing the agent to reuse existing geometry references without re-executing full construction histories7.  
To ensure transaction safety during complex edits, the MCP server pushes the current session state onto an execution history stack prior to every code execution7. If an edit command fails or generates an invalid B-Rep solid, the environment automatically rolls back the stack to restore the previous valid state, preventing state corruption7. In addition, an explicit undo tool allows the agent to revert edits that execute successfully but produce visually or dimensionally unintended results7.

Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that stateful execution environments significantly boost performance across open-weight and proprietary models7. By isolating code modifications within a persistent namespace and providing rollback guarantees, open-source models like Qwen3.6-27B achieve a nearly twofold increase in edit validity and a sevenfold increase in user acceptance7.

## **Physics-Aware Synthesis, FEA Feedback, and Dynamic Mechanical Assemblies**

A major trend in agentic CAD research is the transition from purely geometric shape matching to physics-validated engineering design4. Traditional CAD benchmarks grade models based on Chamfer distance or visual similarity relative to a ground-truth mesh4. However, in real-world engineering, parts that appear visually correct may fail under mechanical loads, exhibit invalid stress distribution paths, or contain interfering assembly interfaces9.  
To bridge the gap between geometric synthesis and physical performance, self-improving CAD agent frameworks reframe part generation as an iterative, simulation-guided optimization process9. Instead of relying solely on visual feedback, the agent interacts with open-source Finite Element Analysis (FEA) solvers—such as CalculiX—to evaluate structural behavior under realistic operational loads9.  
This physics-aware generation workflow operates across three main stages9:

* In the Pre-CAD Blueprint Stage, the agent converts a free-form engineering brief into a structured contract (e.g., Schema-v4 specification)9. This contract fixes bounding envelopes, establishes interface mating surfaces, and declares auditable parametric primitives alongside required functional targets before emitting code9.  
* In the Multi-View Visual Inspection Stage, an automated rendering engine generates 21 calibrated views of the STEP artifact exported by CadQuery9. These views include orthographic projections, close-ups of interface features, and internal X-ray cross-sections, providing the agent with comprehensive visual feedback without requiring manual viewer interaction9.  
* In the Automated FEA Feedback Loop, the verified STEP file is meshed and passed to the CalculiX solver under pre-configured boundary conditions9. The solver evaluates physical criteria—including maximum von Mises stress, displacement, buckling modes, natural resonance frequencies, and clearance tolerances—and returns a typed, structured failure report to the agent9.

On the Hephaestus-CCX benchmark, scaling test-time compute through simulation feedback loops yields continuous structural improvements9. Extending the feedback loop from 10 minutes to 70 minutes of agent compute enables models to incrementally eliminate stress concentrations and wall-thickness defects, converting physically non-viable models into fully compliant industrial parts9.  
In parallel with physics-aware single-part design, agentic CAD has expanded into multi-part dynamic assemblies featuring movable kinematic links8. Generating functional mechanisms requires solving complex spatial constraint networks to ensure component motion along intended degrees of freedom without mechanical binding or interference8.  
By modifying FreeCAD's core execution environment and integrating an assembly constraint solver into the agent's tool set, agentic systems can build dynamic 3D assemblies that pass functional mechanical tests, such as the operational "scissors test"8. The modified solver provides spatial cues and detailed error feedback whenever constraints are over-constrained, under-constrained, or kinematically locked8. Complementary systems, such as ArtiCAD and shared relational DSL platforms, extend this capacity by maintaining joint-enabled part trees, allowing agents to simultaneously generate B-Rep solid geometries and specify their rotational or translational kinematic joints10.

## **Domain-Specific Languages, Solver Integration, and TCAD Automation**

Direct LLM code generation often suffers from spatial reasoning limits when models attempt to calculate complex 3D coordinate intersections or geometric transformations directly11. Forcing language models to perform precise floating-point arithmetic leads to cumulative spatial drift11. To address this challenge, recent research emphasizes joint agent-DSL co-design, offloading spatial calculations to external geometric solvers10.  
Language representations like AIDL (A Solver-Aided Hierarchical Language for LLM-Driven CAD) restructure how agents specify geometric entities11. AIDL incorporates four core design principles tailored to LLM reasoning11:

* Symbolic Constraint Declarations: Instead of outputting absolute vertex coordinates, the agent declares symbolic geometric relationships (e.g., coincident, tangent, parallel, concentric), leaving exact numerical evaluation to an underlying constraint solver11.  
* Implicit Reference Resolution: Primitives use intuitive named variables and semantic handles (such as top\_left or center\_bore)11. Referencing these named handles implicitly enforces positional constraints, preserving design intent when intermediate dimensions are modified during downstream edits11.  
* Hierarchical Constraint Decoupling: Constraints are structured hierarchically, enabling local sketch-level constraints to be solved before executing global 3D extrusions or boolean operations, isolating topological errors and preventing solver divergence11.  
* Explicit Modular Abstraction: Design features are encapsulated into reusable modules, lowering structural complexity and enabling incremental editing11.

By leveraging solver-aided DSLs, language models focus on high-level relational topology and semantic structure, while offloading numerical precision to deterministic constraint solvers10.  
The principles of multi-agent CAD automation have also expanded into sub-micron semiconductor device design through frameworks such as AgenticTCAD6. Semiconductor Technology CAD (TCAD) requires writing complex simulation scripts to model fabrication processes, ion implantation, etching, and electron transport equations6.  
AgenticTCAD combines domain-specific Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with a multi-agent optimization workflow linked to commercial TCAD solvers6. The framework optimizes devices based on high-level electrical targets through two key mechanisms6:

* Automated Physical Diagnostics: Following simulation execution, a post-processing module extracts key physical diagnostics, such as energy band diagrams across the transistor channel region—including conduction band (![][image5]), valence band (![][image6]), electron quasi-Fermi level (![][image7]), and hole quasi-Fermi level (![][image8])6.  
* Trajectory Guidance Dynamics: Experiments reveal that prompting strategy directly impacts optimization stability6. Qualitative guidance prompts often cause parameter oscillation, whereas quantitative, gradient-informed guidance enables the reasoning agent to steadily converge on physical target parameters6.

In validation tests on a 2 nm Nanosheet Field-Effect Transistor (NS-FET) design, AgenticTCAD met International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS)-2024 specifications within 4.2 hours6. Human experts using traditional commercial tool interfaces required 7.1 days to reach the same baseline, demonstrating a substantial acceleration in semiconductor development cycles6.

## **Evaluation Benchmarks, Verification Hierarchies, and Unsupervised Consensus**

As agentic CAD systems mature, evaluation methodologies are evolving from simple visual shape-matching metrics toward multi-tiered benchmarks testing parametric integrity, editability, and manufacturability4.  
Standardized evaluation frameworks now establish multi-tier testing protocols4:

* Text2CAD-Bench provides 600 human-curated examples organized across four geometric complexity levels16. Each sample includes dual natural language descriptions: geometric descriptions (focusing on visual spatial appearance) and sequence descriptions (specifying step-by-step construction operations)16. This dual-style format measures model robustness across different user prompting styles16.  
* CADEngBench-P (and BenchCAD) establishes a multi-tier verification hierarchy designed for industrial programmatic models4:  
  * Level 0 (L0) tests Program and Solid Validity, verifying whether generated code compiles, creates valid non-manifold B-Rep solids, exports to STEP format, and re-imports cleanly without topological errors4.  
  * Level 1 (L1) evaluates Design for Manufacturing (DFM) compliance, checking manufacturing constraints such as minimum wall thickness, tool clearance, and draft angles4.  
  * Level 2 (L2) measures Parameter Perturbation (![][image9]) and Functional Editing (![][image10]), testing whether parameter changes rebuild cleanly while preserving protected feature geometry4.  
  * Level 3 (L3) executes physical simulation checks via CalculiX FEA to evaluate structural stress and deflection under operational loads4.

In open-ended text-to-CAD generation, ground-truth reference models are rarely available to evaluate output quality17. To address this, recent research introduces training-free Unsupervised Geometric Consensus Selection17.  
Given a pool of ![][image11] CAD programs generated from an ambiguous prompt, the framework normalizes and spatially aligns all successfully compiled 3D meshes into a shared coordinate frame17. It then measures inter-candidate geometric agreement using pairwise Chamfer distances or Volumetric IoU17. Candidates situated at the central medoid of the geometric distribution represent the most stable structural interpretations of the prompt17. Selecting candidates via geometric consensus yields a 1% to 10% reduction in Chamfer distance compared to random candidate selection, establishing an effective unsupervised quality filter for agentic CAD workflows17.

| **CAD2Program** \[cite: 3\] | 2D Drawing to 3D Part | Visual Feature Embeddings \+ Code Syntax Parsers | ViT-MLP-LLM translation without numerical quantization loss | High 3D reconstruction fidelity from orthographic views3 |

The rapid development of agentic CAD highlights a broader shift in engineering software architecture1. Monolithic neural networks that attempt to generate raw 3D geometry in a single forward pass are increasingly being replaced by agentic frameworks that orchestrate specialized tools, execution environments, and physics solvers1.  
By decoupling high-level design intent from low-level geometric solving, integrating stateful runtime harnesses, and incorporating real-time physical simulation feedback, agentic systems are overcoming the reliability limitations of early text-to-3D models1. As computational latency in FEA loops decreases and tool integration across commercial CAD platforms improves, these agentic architectures are set to evolve from design assistants into fully autonomous engineering systems capable of generating verified, manufacturable industrial assets1.
